column1: Reconstruct the First Way: from motion (ST Ia Q2 a3; SCG I.13).
column2:
Aim: a first mover, moved by no other, on which every change depends here and now.
Premises: some things are in motion; "motion is nothing else than the reduction of something from potentiality to actuality" (ST Ia Q2 a3); only what is in act actualizes; nothing is in act and potency in the same respect, so "whatever is in motion must be put in motion by another"; the series cannot go to infinity, since later movers move only as moved by the first, "as the staff moves only because it is put in motion by the hand" (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Conclusion: "it is necessary to arrive at a first mover, put in motion by no other; and this everyone understands to be God" (ST Ia Q2 a3). The series excluded is per se (vertical), not per accidens (Ia Q46 a2 ad 7).
Objections: Newton's inertia; an infinite series leaves nothing unexplained (Oberle).
Reply (the literature's): "motion" is any potency being actualized, not only change of place; in a per se series power is only borrowed, so a series of borrowers explains nothing (Cameron). SEP: the dispute "hinges in part on the distinction between per se and per accidens series". Open.

column1: Reconstruct the Second Way: from efficient causes (ST Ia Q2 a3; SCG I.13).
column2:
Aim: a first, uncaused efficient cause on which every other cause depends for its causing.
Premises: "In the world of sense we find there is an order of efficient causes"; nothing causes itself, "for so it would be prior to itself, which is impossible"; in an ordered series the first causes the intermediate and the intermediate the last; "Now to take away the cause is to take away the effect" (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Conclusion: "it is necessary to admit a first efficient cause, to which everyone gives the name of God" (ST Ia Q2 a3). Valid only for a per se series: a line of fathers may be infinite, since a man begets "as a man, and not as the son of another man" (Ia Q46 a2 ad 7).
Objection: the Hume-Edwards principle: explain each member and the whole is explained (Hume, Dialogues part 9); Russell: the universe is "just there, and that's all".
Reply (the literature's): the principle fits per accidens series, not per se ones, where no member has the power passed along; Rowe: explaining each dependent being is not explaining "why there are dependent beings at all". Sobel and Oppy contest per se sustaining causes. Open.

column1: Reconstruct the Third Way: from possibility and necessity (ST Ia Q2 a3).
column2:
Aim: something exists necessarily, and one thing has its necessity of itself. "Necessary" means unable to cease to exist (Kenny), not logical necessity.
Premises: some things are "possible to be and not to be", being generated and corrupting; "that which is possible not to be at some time is not"; so "if everything is possible not to be, then at one time there could have been nothing in existence"; then nothing would exist now; things exist, so something is necessary; necessary things caused by others cannot go to infinity (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Conclusion: a being "having of itself its own necessity", causing necessity in others; "This all men speak of as God" (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Objection: the quantifier shift (Plantinga, Kenny, Rowe): from each perishable thing failing at some time it does not follow that at some time all fail. Rundle: conserved matter-energy is necessary in Kenny's sense.
Reply (the literature's): defend the temporal reading and its principle; or Haldane's atemporal reading (dependence now); or rest on step 6 alone, which also answers Rundle. Library entry: "best studied as an open argument, not a closed one".

column1: Reconstruct the Fourth Way: from gradation (ST Ia Q2 a3; SCG I.13).
column2:
Aim: something best, truest and most fully a being, which causes every perfection in other things.
Premises: "Among beings there are some more and some less good, true, noble and the like"; more and less are said by resemblance to a maximum; so there is "something which is uttermost being"; "the maximum in any genus is the cause of all in that genus" (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Conclusion: there is "something which is to all beings the cause of their being, goodness, and every other perfection; and this we call God" (ST Ia Q2 a3). The metaphysics behind it is participation (Ia Q44 a1).
Objections: comparison needs no real maximum (Dawkins's supreme stinker); the hottest thing need not cause heat; God is in no genus (Ia Q3 a5).
Reply (the literature's): the argument concerns transcendentals (being, good, true) that admit an unlimited case, not height or smell (Ward); a limited degree shows the perfection is had by sharing; "genus" is loose, since creatures resemble God "solely according to analogy" (Ia Q4 a3 ad 3). The Way is only as strong as participation and analogy.

column1: Reconstruct the Fifth Way: from the governance of things (ST Ia Q2 a3; SCG I.13).
column2:
Aim: an intelligent being directs natural things that lack knowledge to their ends.
Premises: "things which lack intelligence, such as natural bodies, act for an end"; they act "always, or nearly always, in the same way"; "whatever lacks intelligence cannot move towards an end, unless it be directed by some being endowed with knowledge and intelligence; as the arrow is shot to its mark by the archer" (ST Ia Q2 a3).
Conclusion: "some intelligent being exists by whom all natural things are directed to their end; and this being we call God" (ST Ia Q2 a3). Not Paley's design argument: it starts from any steady tendency (Aristotle's final cause), not from complex contrivance.
Objection: Aquinas's own obj. 2: all natural things reduce to "one principle which is nature"; Darwin; Hume: nothing shows the cause is one, wise or good.
Reply: Aquinas's own (ad 2): nature works "under the direction of a higher agent". The literature's (Feser): selection presupposes regular causal directedness. Critics: "acts for an end" is a metaphor for regularity. Open.

column1: Reconstruct the real distinction of essence and existence (De ente et essentia ch. 4; ST Ia Q3 a4).
column2:
Aim: in every creature essence and esse differ as potency and act; only one thing is its own existence, and it causes existence in all else.
Premises: (1) every essence can be understood without knowing whether it exists (the phoenix), so existence is other than essence unless some thing's quiddity is its existence; (2) subsistent existence could not be multiplied by a difference or by matter, so it "can only be one and first" (dossier's gloss); (3) nothing causes its own existence, so whatever has existence other than its essence "has existence from another" (gloss), and the regress must end.
Conclusion: a first cause that is esse tantum, "the first cause, which is God" (gloss); a creature's essence is in potency to the existence it receives.
Objections: stage one shows only a conceptual distinction (Morning and Evening star); Fregean: existence is no ingredient; Suárez: distinct by reason only.
Reply: readings divide (IEP): Patt, Kenny, Long: stage one aims at a real distinction; Wippel: stage two settles it; Owens: stage three. Aquinas's own, against the Fregean: "to be" means the act of essence or the composition of a proposition (Ia Q3 a4 ad 2). Open.

column1: Reconstruct the case for divine simplicity (ST Ia Q3).
column2:
Aim: God has no composition of any kind; God is, rather than has, goodness, wisdom and existence.
Premises: God is not a body (he is pure act), so not matter and form, nor a nature in an individual; his essence is his existence, else he would have it from another, "But this cannot be true of God; because we call God the first efficient cause" (Ia Q3 a4); so he is in no genus and has no accidents; "every composite is posterior to its component parts"; "every composite has a cause ... But God is uncaused" (Ia Q3 a7).
Conclusion: God "is nowise composite, but is altogether simple" (ST Ia Q3 a7).
Objections: Plantinga (1980): God becomes a property, abstract and inert; modal collapse (Mullins, Leftow): one necessary simple act makes creation necessary.
Reply: Bergmann and Brower's truthmaker reading (the literature's); the names are not synonymous, signifying one thing "under many and different aspects" (Q13 a4); God "wills His own goodness necessarily", other things not, and the contingency lies in the creature (Q19 a3). Critics: restated, not explained. SEP ends in an aporetic postscript.

column1: Reconstruct the analogy of divine names (ST Ia Q13 a5).
column2:
Aim: "good", "wise" and "being" are said of God and creatures analogically, so we speak truly of God without knowing what God is.
Premises: univocal predication fails: in a man "wise" names a perfection distinct from his essence, but said of God it "leaves the thing signified as incomprehended"; pure equivocation fails, else nothing could be demonstrated of God, since "the reasoning would always be exposed to the fallacy of equivocation"; the analogous term "signifies various proportions to some one thing" ("healthy"); creatures relate to God as to their cause (ST Ia Q13 a5).
Conclusion: "these names are said of God and creatures in an analogous sense, i.e. according to proportion" (ST Ia Q13 a5).
Objection: Scotus: an analogical term is one concept (so univocal) or several (so equivocal); "being" must be univocal.
Reply: Aquinas's own: "all univocal predications are reduced to one first non-univocal analogical predication, which is being" (a5 ad 1). The literature's: the order of analogy gives enough unity to avoid equivocation; attribution vs proportionality is disputed (Cajetan; McInerny; Hochschild). Open.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that the eternity of the world cannot be disproved (ST Ia Q46 a2; De aeternitate mundi).
column2:
Aim: reason can prove neither that the world always existed nor that it began; a limit of proof, not a claim about the world's age.
Premises: demonstration starts from essence, but "everything according to its species is abstracted from 'here' and 'now'"; God creates by will, knowable only where he wills of necessity, and he need not will creatures (Q19 a3); the proofs of a beginning fail: from any past day "there is a finite number of days which can be passed through" (ad 6); an accidentally ordered series can be infinite (ad 7) (ST Ia Q46 a2).
Conclusion: "By faith alone do we hold, and by no demonstration can it be proved, that the world did not always exist" (ST Ia Q46 a2). De aeternitate mundi: created and beginningless is no contradiction.
Objection: Bonaventure: made from nothing means being after non-being, so "eternal" and "created" contradict; an infinite past cannot be crossed (now Craig's kalām).
Reply: Aquinas's own: "after nothing" can be an order of nature, not of time; bad proofs give "occasion to unbelievers to laugh". Craig: the whole series is the problem. Open.

column1: Reconstruct evil as privation (ST Ia Q48–49).
column2:
Aim: evil is the lack of a due good, caused only by good acting incidentally; God causes no fault.
Premises: good is the desirable, so being is good; so "by the name of evil is signified the absence of good" (Q48 a1); not every absence, but a privation, as "the privation of sight is called blindness" (a3); a privation needs a good subject; "only good can be a cause" (Q49 a1); God has no defect, so sin is not from him (Q49 a2).
Conclusion: "there is no one first principle of evil, as there is one first principle of good" (Q49 a3), against the Manichees; "God is the author of the evil which is penalty, but not of the evil which is fault" (Q49 a2). The limp: its obliqueness comes from "the curvature of the leg".
Objections: pain seems positive; Mackie, Rowe: what evil is does not explain why God permits it; the lion-and-ass passage (Q48 a2 ad 3) is aesthetic theodicy.
Reply (the literature's): Davies: God is not a moral agent among others; Stump: the goods must be for the sufferer. Aquinas on penalty: the surgeon cuts off a limb to save the body (Q48 a6). Disputed.

column1: Reconstruct the soul as form of the body and the unity of substantial form (ST Ia Q76 a1, a4).
column2:
Aim: the intellectual soul is the body's substantial form, and a human being has only one substantial form.
Premises: what a thing primarily acts by is its form; the soul is what we live, sense and understand by; "each one is conscious that it is himself who understands", and the same one senses, so the person is not the soul alone (against Plato); Averroes' link through images fails: "we do not say that the wall sees, but rather that it is seen" (Q76 a1). Unity (a4): "Of one thing there is but one substantial being"; an earlier substantial form would make the soul accidental.
Conclusion: "this particular man understands, because the intellectual principle is his form" (Q76 a1); "there is no other substantial form in man besides the intellectual soul" (a4).
Objection: the pluralists: the corpse is plainly the same body; Kilwardby's Oxford condemnation (1277).
Reply: Aquinas's own: bite the bullet, only prime matter persists; elements remain "not actually but virtually" (a4 ad 4). On the separated soul, corruptionists (Toner, Van Dyke) vs survivalists (Stump, Brower). Open.

column1: Reconstruct the case against the unity of the intellect (ST Ia Q76 a2; De unitate intellectus).
column2:
Aim: each human has their own possible intellect, against Averroes, argued from philosophy, not faith.
Premises: if the person is the intellect, one intellect makes Socrates and Plato one man, "which is quite absurd"; if the intellect is a power of the body's form, "it is impossible for many distinct individuals to have one form"; one principal agent would leave all men with "but one act of understanding"; many images yield one intelligible species, so they cannot divide the act (ST Ia Q76 a2).
Conclusion: "it is altogether impossible and unreasonable to maintain that there exists one intellect for all men" (ST Ia Q76 a2). De unitate intellectus (1270) argues it mainly from Aristotle's text.
Objection: Averroes: immaterial things cannot be many in a species; an individuated intellect could not know universals; no common object of science.
Reply: Aquinas's own: souls are many "according to the division of matter" (ad 1); materiality, not individuality, blocks universals (ad 3); what is understood is the thing, not the species (ad 4). Whether he reads Aristotle rightly is still divided.

column1: Reconstruct knowledge through phantasms: abstraction (ST Ia Q84 a6–7, Q85 a1).
column2:
Aim: human knowledge begins in the senses; the intellect grasps natures by abstraction from phantasms and always turns back to them.
Premises: intellect and sense are distinct powers; a body cannot act on the incorporeal; so an agent intellect makes phantasms "actually intelligible, by a process of abstraction" (Q84 a6); the proper object is "a quiddity or nature existing in corporeal matter" (Q84 a7); to know it but not as in this matter "is to abstract the form from individual matter which is represented by the phantasms" (Q85 a1).
Conclusion: "our intellect understands material things by abstracting from the phantasms" (Q85 a1), and "it is impossible for our intellect to understand anything actually, except by turning to the phantasms" (Q84 a7).
Objections: Berkeley: abstraction is unintelligible; the agent intellect is a black box (SEP); species threaten a veil of ideas.
Reply: Aquinas's own: the species is "that by which the intellect understands" (Q85 a2). Direct realist (Perler) vs representationalist (Pasnau, Panaccio) readings; abstraction is consideration, not imagery, so Berkeley hits Locke. Open.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that happiness is the vision of God (ST Ia-IIae Q2–3).
column2:
Aim: no created good is the last end; happiness is an act of intellect; perfect happiness is the vision of God, not had in this life.
Premises: happiness is "the perfect good, which lulls the appetite altogether" (Q2 a8); wealth, honour, power and pleasure fail; "naught can lull man's will, save the universal good. This is to be found, not in any creature, but in God alone" (Q2 a8); attaining is an act of intellect, not will, else "the covetous man would have it from the very moment that he wished for it" (Q3 a4); the mind rests only in knowing what a cause is; here we know only that God is.
Conclusion: "Final and perfect happiness can consist in nothing else than the vision of the Divine Essence" (ST Ia-IIae Q3 a8). In this life: "We call men happy, but only as men" (Q3 a2 ad 4).
Objections: Scotus: beatitude lies in the will's love; a natural desire for a supernatural end blurs nature and grace.
Reply: Aquinas's own: delight is happiness's "proper accident" (Q3 a4). On the desire, de Lubac vs the Cajetan tradition (defended by Feingold). Still argued.

column1: Reconstruct the first precept of natural law and its order (ST Ia-IIae Q94 a2).
column2:
Aim: natural law has one self-evident first precept, and its further precepts follow the order of natural inclinations.
Premises: natural-law precepts stand to practical reason as first principles of demonstration to theoretical reason: "both are self-evident principles"; being is first grasped by theoretical reason, good by practical, "since every agent acts for an end under the aspect of good"; "all those things to which man has a natural inclination, are naturally apprehended by reason as being good" (ST Ia-IIae Q94 a2).
Conclusion: the first precept is "good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided"; "according to the order of natural inclinations, is the order of the precepts of the natural law" (Q94 a2): life; mating and offspring; knowing God and living in society.
Objection: Hume's is–ought gap; and the order seems to rank goods by how widely the inclination is shared.
Reply (the literature's): Grisez and Finnis: basic goods are self-evident, not inferred from nature; McInerny and Hittinger: that cuts natural law from Q91's metaphysics. The order is of appearance, not importance; reason rules the lower inclinations (ad 2).

column1: Reconstruct double effect in self-defence (ST IIa-IIae Q64 a7).
column2:
Aim: a private person may use force that kills an attacker if the killing is not intended and the force is proportionate.
Premises: "Nothing hinders one act from having two effects, only one of which is intended, while the other is beside the intention"; "moral acts take their species according to what is intended"; self-defence can save one's life and slay the aggressor; saving one's life is lawful, as "it is natural to everything to keep itself in 'being,' as far as possible"; but an act "may be rendered unlawful, if it be out of proportion to the end"; only public authority may intend to kill (a3) (ST IIa-IIae Q64 a7).
Conclusion: moderate defence is no sin, "since one is bound to take more care of one's own life than of another's" (Q64 a7). Of Mangan's later four conditions, only intention and proportion are explicit here.
Objection: does the article state double effect at all? The problem of closeness (SEP §4.2); consequentialists: intending vs foreseeing has no moral weight.
Reply (the literature's): readings divide (Mangan, Grisez vs an end-only reading; Cavanaugh surveys); Anscombe: the line is real but easily abused. Closeness remains unresolved.

column1: What are act and potency (actus, potentia)?
column2: Actuality and capacity. A cold kettle is actually cold and potentially hot; change is the passage from potency to act in some respect. "For motion is nothing else than the reduction of something from potentiality to actuality. But nothing can be reduced from potentiality to actuality, except by something in a state of actuality" (ST Ia Q2 a3). "Motion" (motus) means change of any kind. Act is prior to potency: a potency is always a potency for some act, and only what is already actual can actualize. The pair reaches beyond physical change: matter is potency for form, a power for its operation, an essence for existence. Its highest use is God as pure act (actus purus), with no potency at all and so unchangeable; "pure act" does not mean busy activity.

column1: What is an essentially ordered (per se) series, and how does it differ from one ordered per accidens?
column2: In a per se series each member causes only while and because it is caused here and now: the hand moves the stick that moves the stone, and each intermediate is a moved mover with borrowed power. In a per accidens series each member has its power in its own right, like a line of fathers and sons, or a smith working with one hammer after another; earlier members need not be acting now (ST Ia Q46 a2 ad 7). "Essentially ordered" is the later label for Aquinas's per se. The Ways argue that a per se series needs a first member; Aquinas does not claim to prove that a temporal series must have had a first member. A per se series is not a chain stretching back in time.

column1: What are matter and form (materia, forma), and substantial versus accidental form?
column2: Hylomorphism: a material thing is a composite of matter, what it is made of, and form, what makes it the kind of thing it is. The substantial form makes this lump of matter a dog and not a stone. Accidental forms, such as size, colour or position, qualify a substance that already exists. Growing or turning grey is accidental change, and the dog remains; death is substantial change: the dog ceases to exist and a corpse comes to be. The form of a house arranges bricks that already exist, so it is accidental and a house is not a substance. A substance has a strong unity an aggregate lacks: a hand cut off is a hand only in name. "Form" is not shape.

column1: What is prime matter (materia prima)?
column2: Matter with no form of its own, pure potency for form, which never exists by itself. It is Aquinas's answer to what persists through a substantial change: when a dog dies, only prime matter carries over into the corpse. It is one of his most debated doctrines; the thesis that prime matter is pure potency was among the propositions condemned at Oxford in 1277 (SEP, "Thomas Aquinas," §9). It supports the unity of substantial form: if a human being has only one substantial form, the corpse is a new substance and strictly only prime matter persists, while apparent sameness is explained by the qualities of the new mixture.

column1: What are essence and existence (essentia, esse), and what is the "real distinction"?
column2: Essence is what a thing is, as expressed by its definition; esse is the act that makes that essence actual (ST Ia Q3 a4). One can understand what a human being or a phoenix is without knowing whether it exists (De ente ch. 4, paraphrased), so in creatures the two differ, as potency and act. "Real distinction" is mostly the commentators' name for the claim that they differ in the thing and not only in thought. Esse is not a property like being red: "existence is that which makes every form or nature actual" (ST Ia Q3 a4). An essence without existence is nothing at all. The doctrine builds on Avicenna and the Book of Causes; whether the distinction is proved real, and at which stage, is debated (Wippel, Owens).

column1: What is subsistent being itself (ipsum esse subsistens)?
column2: God as the one being whose essence is its existence: "Therefore His essence is His existence" (ST Ia Q3 a4). If God's existence differed from his essence, it would be received from a cause, and God is the first cause; it would stand to essence as act to potency, and God has no potency. De ente adds that there can be only one such being, since pure existence could not be multiplied. A hierarchy follows: material things are doubly limited, their essence received in matter and their existence in their essence; angels have no matter, but their existence is still received and limited by their essence; God alone is unreceived existence. The usual Thomist summary: act is limited only by the potency that receives it.

column1: What is participation (participatio)?
column2: Having a perfection, above all existence, received from a source that has it essentially. A creature has existence without being existence, as an iron bar in a forge is on fire without being fire. Hence "all beings apart from God are not their own being, but are beings by participation" (ST Ia Q44 a1). The principle: "whatever is found in anything by participation, must be caused in it by that to which it belongs essentially" (ST Ia Q44 a1). On this view creation is the continuing gift of existence, not only a first event: a creature depends on God at every moment, as the light in the air depends on the sun. Participation is the metaphysics behind the Fourth Way.

column1: What is divine simplicity, and what is the way of remotion?
column2: Simplicity is God's lack of any composition: of parts, matter and form, essence and existence, genus and difference, substance and accident. God "is nowise composite, but is altogether simple" (ST Ia Q3 a7). The way of remotion (negation) is the method that reaches it: knowing God by knowing what God is not. At the start of Q3 Aquinas says we can consider how God is not, rather than how he is, and the denials of Q3 are all negations; Rickaby renders the SCG I.14 term "negative differentiation". Because God has no composition, no human concept, which grasps one feature distinct from others, can capture what God is. The way comes partly from Pseudo-Dionysius and leads straight to the problem of the divine names.

column1: What is the difference between what a divine name signifies and its mode of signifying?
column2: Words such as "good" or "wise" signify a perfection and also carry a creaturely way of signifying it. "As regards what is signified by these names, they belong properly to God, and more properly than they belong to creatures, and are applied primarily to Him. But as regards their mode of signification, they do not properly and strictly apply to God" (ST Ia Q13 a3). Words whose very meaning includes a bodily mode, like "rock" or "lion", apply to God only as metaphors. Article 6 gives the order: as to the thing signified the names apply first to God; as to their imposition, to creatures "which we know first" (Q13 a6). The upshot is a qualified agnosticism: we know that God is wise, not what divine wisdom is.

column1: What is analogy (analogia) in Aquinas's account of the divine names?
column2: A predication neither univocal (same sense) nor purely equivocal (unrelated senses, like "bank"), but by proportion to one source. "Univocal predication is impossible between God and creatures" (ST Ia Q13 a5), because a perfection divided and limited in creatures is undivided and unlimited in God. Pure equivocation would wreck every argument from creatures to God. So "these names are said of God and creatures in an analogous sense, i.e. according to proportion" (ST Ia Q13 a5), as "healthy" is said of an animal, of medicine and of urine. The ground is causal: creatures resemble God as effects resemble a cause that exceeds them. "Analogy of proper proportionality" is Cajetan's later classification, not Aquinas's term; Scotus answered with the univocity of being.

column1: What is sacred doctrine (sacra doctrina), and why does it count as a science?
column2: The teaching based on revelation, wider than the later academic subject "theology". It is needed because humans are directed to an end, the vision of God, that exceeds reason, and because otherwise "the truth about God such as reason could discover, would only be known by a few, and that after a long time, and with the admixture of many errors" (ST Ia Q1 a1). It is a science in Aristotle's sense because it reasons from principles to conclusions, though its principles are known to a higher knower: "sacred doctrine is a science because it proceeds from principles established by the light of a higher science, namely, the science of God and the blessed" (ST Ia Q1 a2), as optics takes its principles from geometry.

column1: What are the preambles of faith (praeambula fidei), and how do they differ from the articles of faith?
column2: The truths that we confess concerning God fall under two modes (SCG I.3, tr. Rickaby). Preambles are truths faith presupposes that reason can prove, such as God's existence and unity; philosophers have demonstrated them, though most believers hold them on faith for lack of time or training (ST IIa-IIae Q2 a4, paraphrased). The label is the later Thomists'. Articles of faith, such as the Trinity, exceed reason entirely. The two cannot conflict: "it is impossible for the truth of faith to be contrary to principles known by natural reason" (SCG I.7, tr. Rickaby). So arguments against the faith "cannot be demonstrations, but are difficulties that can be answered" (ST Ia Q1 a8).

column1: What does "grace does not destroy nature but perfects it" mean for Aquinas?
column2: Grace (gratia) is God's created gift that heals nature and lifts it toward a supernatural end (ST Ia-IIae Q109); it does not replace nature. "Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity" (ST Ia Q1 a8 ad 2). Fallen nature cannot do even all the natural good it is capable of without help: it needs "the help of grace to heal his nature" (Ia-IIae Q109 a3). Later scholastics label the two jobs healing and elevating grace. The pattern runs through the system: philosophy within theology, acquired under infused virtue, natural under divine law, the natural end under the supernatural; the higher completes the lower without cancelling it.

column1: What is creation (creatio) in Aquinas's strict sense?
column2: Giving existence to a thing from nothing, with no prior matter or subject. Only God can do it, since only the being whose essence is existence can give existence as such (ST Ia Q45). It is not a change, because a change needs something that persists; it is a relation of dependence on God in the creature. This separates two questions: whether the world depends on God, which can be proved, and whether it had a beginning in time, which cannot be proved either way: "Hence that the world began to exist is an object of faith, but not of demonstration or science" (ST Ia Q46 a2). Proving creation does not require proving a first moment, which is why the Five Ways concern present dependence.

column1: What are the transcendentals, and why are being and good the same?
column2: Being, one, true and good, which apply across every category; the sense has nothing to do with Kant's later one, and the class label is the later Thomists' (Aquinas lists them in De veritate Q1 a1). "Goodness and being are really the same, and differ only in idea" (ST Ia Q5 a1): a thing is good insofar as it is desirable, desirable insofar as perfect, perfect insofar as in act, that is, insofar as it exists. "Good" adds a relation to desire. Being comes first: "the first thing conceived by the intellect is being" (ST Ia Q5 a2), and the others add a relation or a negation to it. Consequences: evil cannot be a being, and the Fourth Way's perfections are transcendentals, not qualities like heat.

column1: What is privation (privatio), and how does it differ from negation?
column2: The absence of a good that ought to be present. A stone's lack of sight is mere negation; an animal's is privation: "the absence of good, taken in a privative sense, is an evil; as, for instance, the privation of sight is called blindness" (ST Ia Q48 a3). Otherwise "a man would be evil who had not the swiftness of the roe, or the strength of a lion" (Q48 a3). Since being as such is good, evil is no being or nature: "by the name of evil is signified the absence of good" (Q48 a1), and it exists only in a good subject. Evil in voluntary agents splits into fault (culpa) and penalty (poena); God causes penalty but never fault (Q49 a2). This sharpens Augustine's privatio boni.

column1: What is a phantasm (phantasma), and what is the turning to the phantasms?
column2: A sense image of a particular thing, held in the internal senses, chiefly imagination, which combine and store what the external senses receive. The intellect abstracts from phantasms and must turn back to them even to use knowledge it already has: "it is impossible for our intellect to understand anything actually, except by turning to the phantasms" (ST Ia Q84 a7). The evidence: damage to a bodily organ stops a person understanding what they already knew, and anyone trying to understand something forms phantasms "to serve him by way of examples" (Q84 a7). This conversio ad phantasmata is why natural theology argues from sensible effects to God, never from a definition of God, and why Aquinas rejects Anselm's argument as a proof for us.

column1: What are the agent intellect and the possible intellect (intellectus agens, intellectus possibilis)?
column2: A phantasm is particular and material; a concept is universal and immaterial. So a power is needed that makes what is potentially intelligible in sense images actually intelligible: the agent intellect. The possible (receptive) intellect, at first like a tablet on which nothing is written (ST Ia Q79 a2), receives the intelligible species and is actualized by it. Both belong to each human soul: "The active intellect, of which the Philosopher speaks, is something in the soul" (ST Ia Q79 a4). Against Averroes, the possible intellect is not one for all humans (Q76 a2). Aquinas keeps Augustine's language of illumination but makes the light the agent intellect, a created share in God's light (Q84 a5).

column1: What is free choice (liberum arbitrium) for Aquinas?
column2: The power of choosing, grounded in reason's judgment not being fixed to one option. The will, the appetite that follows the intellect, wills happiness, the good as such, necessarily, but no particular good necessarily, since none is so tied to happiness that one cannot be happy without it (ST Ia Q82 a1–2). A sheep flees the wolf by a natural judgment fixed to one outcome; a human being compares reasons, and in contingent matters reason can go either way. "And forasmuch as man is rational is it necessary that man have a free-will" (ST Ia Q83 a1). It is not identical with modern libertarian free will: whether Aquinas is a compatibilist (Kenny, Pasnau) or a libertarian (Stump) is disputed.

column1: What is happiness (beatitudo) for Aquinas, and how does imperfect happiness differ from perfect?
column2: The last end of human life, which everyone wants under the name "happiness" though people disagree about what it is (Ia-IIae Q1 a4–7). Not a feeling of well-being. "It is impossible for any created good to constitute man's happiness" (ST Ia-IIae Q2 a8), since the will's object is the universal good, God. Happiness as possessing that good is an act of the intellect: "Final and perfect happiness can consist in nothing else than the vision of the Divine Essence" (ST Ia-IIae Q3 a8). Imperfect happiness, possible in this life, lies in contemplation and virtuous action, which Aristotle described (Q3 a2 ad 4; Q5 a3). Perfect happiness exceeds every created nature and is God's gift (Q5 a5).

column1: What is a habit (habitus), and what is virtue?
column2: A stable disposition between a power and its acts that makes the power act well or badly with ease; not "habit" in the sense of a mindless routine. Virtue is a good habit: "human virtue which is an operative habit, is a good habit, productive of good works" (ST Ia-IIae Q55 a3). Intellectual virtues perfect the intellect: understanding, scientific knowledge, wisdom, art and prudence. Moral virtues perfect the appetites; the four cardinal ones (Latin cardo, a hinge) are prudence, justice, fortitude and temperance (Q61). Prudence is intellectual by its subject and moral by its matter, and no moral virtue exists without it, which is why the moral virtues are connected (Q58 a4, Q65 a1, paraphrased).

column1: What are the theological virtues, and why are they needed?
column2: Faith, hope and charity. Human beings have two ends: a happiness proportionate to human nature, and "a happiness surpassing man's nature, and which man can obtain by the power of God alone, by a kind of participation of the Godhead" (ST Ia-IIae Q62 a1). Natural powers, however well trained, are not proportioned to the second, so God gives further principles that have God as their object and are infused, not acquired by practice. With charity God also infuses moral virtues distinct in kind from the acquired ones Aristotle describes (Q63 a3–4). Charity is "a kind of friendship of man for God" (ST IIa-IIae Q23 a5) and the form of all the virtues, directing their acts to the last end (Q23 a8, paraphrased).

column1: What is law, and what is natural law (lex naturalis)?
column2: Law is "an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by him who has care of the community, and promulgated" (ST Ia-IIae Q90 a4): a work of reason, not bare will; for the common good, not the ruler's private good; by a proper author; made known. Eternal law is God's governing reason for the universe. Non-rational things share in it by being moved; rational creatures share in it by understanding it and directing themselves: "this participation of the eternal law in the rational creature is called the natural law" (Q91 a2). Natural law is not a set of biological regularities or a code written in nature; it is human practical reason itself, seen as a share in God's reason. Its first precept: "good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided" (Q94 a2).

column1: What is synderesis, and how does it differ from conscience?
column2: Synderesis is the natural habit by which practical reason holds the first principles of natural law (ST Ia Q79 a12). Conscience is not a habit but an act, applying knowledge to a particular case (Ia Q79 a13). The first principles held by synderesis stand to practical reason as non-contradiction stands to theoretical reason: "both are self-evident principles" (ST Ia-IIae Q94 a2). Those first principles are the same for all; the more detailed conclusions hold only in most cases and can be obscured by bad custom (Q94 a4–6).

column1: What is the disputed-question form of an article of the Summa?
column2: Each article states objections, a counter-authority (sed contra), Aquinas's answer (respondeo) and replies to the objections; "ad 2" is the reply to the second objection. The form came from the university practice of public disputation at Paris, where masters of theology were required to dispute as well as lecture and preach. The objections are not Aquinas's view, and the replies can carry as much doctrine as the answer: the Fifth Way's ad 2 meets the naturalist objection, and the replies of Ia Q46 a2 do most of the work against proofs of a beginning. Learn the four steps before reading any argument.
